answer: Decision thresholds, also called willingness-to-pay thresholds, translate cost-effectiveness ratios into funding decisions. A threshold sets the maximum a payer is willing to spend for one additional quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Programs whose incremental cost-effectiveness ratio falls below the threshold are considered worth funding, while those above it are not. Because health gains and costs differ across competing programs, the threshold acts as a consistent decision rule that separates good value from poor value, though uncertainty in the underlying estimates can move a program across the line.

faqs.q: What is a willingness-to-pay threshold in health economics?
faqs.a: It is the maximum amount a payer is willing to spend to gain one additional QALY. Programs with a cost per QALY below the threshold are judged worth funding; those above it are not.

faqs.q: How do thresholds turn ICERs into policy decisions?
faqs.a: By comparing each program's incremental cost-effectiveness ratio to the threshold, decision-makers convert a dollar-per-QALY figure into a fund or do-not-fund recommendation using a consistent rule across competing programs.

faqs.q: How does uncertainty affect threshold-based decisions?
faqs.a: Because cost and effect estimates are uncertain, a program near the threshold may be cost-effective under one set of assumptions and not under another, so the funding decision can shift when inputs are varied.
